subject: chemical
audience: FE Chemical candidates and chemical engineering students
title: The Rate Constant That Increased Sixfold at 330 K
featured_title: THE RATE CONSTANT THAT INCREASED SIXFOLD AT 330 K

presentation.challenge: A 30 K temperature rise did not cause a 10% kinetic change. The Arrhenius relation increased the rate constant by a factor of about 6.19.

practice.primary_question: How does the Arrhenius equation predict the change in a reaction rate constant with temperature?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating temperature effects on the rate constant as linear or using Celsius values in reciprocal-temperature terms.

case_dna.target_misconception: Raising temperature from 300 K to 330 K increases a rate constant by roughly 10% because temperature rises by 10%.
case_dna.why_plausible: Linear proportional reasoning is common, but the Arrhenius law depends exponentially on reciprocal absolute temperature.
case_dna.corrected_model: Use ln(k2/k1)=-(Ea/R)(1/T2-1/T1) with Ea and R in consistent units and T in kelvin.

problem_statement: A reaction has k1=0.10 min^-1 at 300 K and activation energy Ea=50 kJ/mol. Estimate k2 at 330 K using R=8.314 J/(mol·K). A note assumes the 10% temperature increase gives k2=0.11 min^-1. Determine the correct rate constant.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The temperature increase was modest. The kinetic response was not.
gates.prompt: Which temperature scale belongs in reciprocal-temperature terms?

options.label: Use ln(k2/k1)=-(Ea/R)(1/T2-1/T1)
options.reason: This eliminates the pre-exponential factor and compares the two temperatures directly.

options.label: Scale k directly by T2/T1
options.reason: The Arrhenius relation is exponential in reciprocal absolute temperature, not linear in T.

options.label: Use reciprocal Celsius temperatures
options.reason: Thermodynamic temperature must be expressed on an absolute scale.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the rate constant at 330 K

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Evaluate the Arrhenius temperature shift
gates.result: The rate constant at 330 K is about 0.619 min^-1.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the new rate constant
gates.hint: Convert 50 kJ/mol to 50,000 J/mol before using R=8.314 J/(mol·K).

cards.text: 1/330-1/300 is negative, so increasing temperature makes ln(k2/k1) positive.
The calculated ratio k2/k1 is about 6.19.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the kinetic-temperature note
report: C1. Temperature rises from 300 K to 330 K.
C2. The activation energy is 50 kJ/mol.
C3. A 10% temperature rise makes the rate constant 10% larger.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: This is the stated activation energy.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It assumes linear proportionality instead of Arrhenius behavior.

evidence_choices.label: k2/k1≈6.19 from the Arrhenius ratio
evidence_choices.reason: This uses the given activation energy and absolute temperatures.

correction.template: The rate constant at 330 K is about {rate_constant} min^-1.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Estimate the first-order half-life at 330 K

options.label: About 6.93 min
options.reason: That is the half-life at k=0.10 min^-1, before the temperature increase.

options.label: About 0.62 min
options.reason: This confuses the rate constant with a time.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the Arrhenius ratio at 315 K
gates.prompt: Using the same k1, Ea, and T1, what is k at 315 K?

options.label: About 0.260 min^-1
options.reason: The Arrhenius ratio is about 2.598, giving k≈0.2598 min^-1.

options.label: 0.105 min^-1
options.reason: That uses nearly linear temperature scaling.

options.label: 0.619 min^-1
options.reason: That is the result at 330 K, not 315 K.

gates.explanation: Arrhenius temperature sensitivity remains exponential for the same activation energy.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the Arrhenius calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that rate constants must be compared with the Arrhenius relation using absolute temperature and consistent energy units.

items.label: What failed
items.value: A linear percentage-temperature rule was applied to reaction kinetics.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Rate constants vary exponentially with reciprocal absolute temperature.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use the Arrhenius ratio with kelvin and consistent Ea/R units.

seo.excerpt: Reaction rate constants do not usually scale linearly with temperature. The Arrhenius equation captures the exponential sensitivity.

faqs.q: Why must temperature be in kelvin in the Arrhenius equation?
faqs.a: The equation uses reciprocal absolute temperature, so an absolute temperature scale is required.
